## Example

Let $\Lambda$ be a full complex lattice with Weierstrass function $\wp$, and
let $z\in\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$ satisfy $\wp'(z)\ne0$. Then
$$\wp(2z)=-2\wp(z)+\frac14\left(\frac{\wp''(z)}{\wp'(z)}\right)^{2}.$$
Moreover $\wp''=6\wp^{2}-\tfrac12g_2$ on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$, so on the
same locus the duplication value is the rational expression
$$-2\wp(z)+\frac{(6\wp(z)^2-\frac12g_2)^2}{4\,\wp'(z)^2}$$
in $\wp(z)$ and $\wp'(z)$. Both identities extend beyond their apparent
exceptional points: the second extends holomorphically to the half-periods
where $\wp'$ vanishes, and the first is an identity of meromorphic functions
on $\mathbb C$ that asserts no finite value at the genuine poles.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A full complex lattice $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\omega_1+\mathbb Z\omega_2$ with oriented basis, its Weierstrass function $\wp$ and derivative $\wp'$, the invariants $g_2=60G_4$, $g_3=140G_6$, and a point $z\in\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$.

[F1] $\wp$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$, is even and $\Lambda$-periodic, and at each lattice point has a double pole with principal part $(z-\lambda)^{-2}$ and no other poles; $\wp'(z)=-2\sum_{\omega\in\Lambda}(z-\omega)^{-3}$ on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$, this series being normally convergent there, and $\wp'$ is odd and $\Lambda$-periodic with a pole of order $3$ at each lattice point ([[thm-weierstrass-p-normal-convergence-and-periodicity]], [[def-weierstrass-elliptic-p-function]]).

[F2] $\wp(z)=\wp(w)$ if and only if $w\equiv z$ or $w\equiv-z$ modulo $\Lambda$; the zeros of $\wp'$ are exactly the $\Lambda$-translates of the three nonzero half-periods, and each of them is of order one; consequently, for $w\in\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$, $\wp'(w)=0$ if and only if $2w\in\Lambda$ ([[lem-weierstrass-p-degree-two-and-half-periods]]).

[F3] $(\wp')^2=4\wp^3-g_2\wp-g_3$ on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$ ([[thm-weierstrass-p-differential-equation]]).

[F4] The addition formula holds meromorphically in $(z,w)$: it holds as an equality of values wherever the displayed quotient is defined, and all apparent exceptional cases are interpreted by meromorphic continuation, without assigning a finite value at a genuine pole ([[thm-weierstrass-p-addition-formula]]).

[F5] A holomorphic function with a zero of order $m$ at $a$ factors near $a$ as $(z-a)^mg(z)$ with $g(a)\ne0$; a holomorphic function on a domain that is not identically zero has isolated zeros; and two holomorphic functions on a domain agreeing on a set with an accumulation point in the domain agree everywhere ([[thm-zero-order-factorization-holomorphic-function]], [[thm-isolated-zeros-holomorphic-function]], [[thm-identity-theorem-holomorphic-functions]]).

[F6] Complex derivatives are linear, satisfy the product rule and the chain rule, and a complex-differentiable function is continuous ([[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]], [[cor-complex-differentiability-implies-continuity]]).

[F7] Meromorphic functions on a connected plane domain form a field: sums, products and quotients with nonzero denominator are meromorphic, and the pole set of a meromorphic function is discrete and closed; a meromorphic function on a domain that vanishes on a nonempty open subset is identically zero ([[def-meromorphic-function-complex-domain]], [[cor-meromorphic-functions-on-a-domain-form-a-field]], [[thm-poles-meromorphic-function-are-discrete-and-countable]]).

[F8] The complex plane is a connected plane domain ([[def-complex-lattice-and-complex-torus]]).

## Verification

1.1 (The second-derivative identity on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$.) Differentiating [F3] with the rules of [F6] gives $2\wp'\wp''=(12\wp^2-g_2)\wp'$ on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$; at every point with $\wp'\ne0$ this gives $\wp''=6\wp^2-\tfrac12g_2$. Let $h\notin\Lambda$ with $\wp'(h)=0$: by [F2] the zero of $\wp'$ at $h$ is of order one, so [F5] gives $\wp'(w)=(w-h)g(w)$ with $g(h)\ne0$, and hence $\wp'(w)\ne0$ for $0<|w-h|<\rho$ with some $\rho>0$; shrinking $\rho$ if necessary, the pole set of the meromorphic function $\wp$ is discrete by [F7], so the disc $D(h,\rho)$ contains no lattice point. Both $\wp''$ and $6\wp^2-\tfrac12g_2$ are holomorphic on $D(h,\rho)$ and agree on the punctured disc $D(h,\rho)\setminus\{h\}$, which is a nonempty connected open set, so [F5] makes them agree on all of $D(h,\rho)$, in particular at $h$. Every point of $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$ either has $\wp'\ne0$ or is such a zero $h$ by [F2], so $\wp''=6\wp^2-\tfrac12g_2$ on all of $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

1.2 (The duplication identity where $\wp'(z)\ne0$.) Fix $z\in\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$ with $\wp'(z)\ne0$; then $2z\notin\Lambda$ by [F2], and $\wp$ is holomorphic near $2z$. By the discreteness of the poles of $\wp$ and of the zeros of $\wp'$ [F2, F7], choose $\rho>0$ so small that $D(z,\rho)$ contains no lattice point, no point of $z+\Lambda$ and no point of $-z+\Lambda$ and so that $z+w\notin\Lambda$ for $w\in D(z,\rho)$; then for $0<|w-z|<\rho$ the addition formula [F4] applies and gives $\wp(z+w)=-\wp(z)-\wp(w)+\tfrac14Q(w)^2$ with $Q(w)=(\wp'(z)-\wp'(w))/(\wp(z)-\wp(w))$. Both $\wp'(z)-\wp'(w)$ and $\wp(z)-\wp(w)$ vanish at $w=z$ and have nonzero derivative there, namely $-\wp''(z)$ and $-\wp'(z)$ with $\wp'(z)\ne0$; by [F5] they factor as $\wp'(z)-\wp'(w)=(z-w)\beta(w)$ and $\wp(z)-\wp(w)=(z-w)\alpha(w)$ with $\alpha(z)=-\wp'(z)\ne0$, so $Q$ extends to a holomorphic function on $D(z,\rho)$ with $Q(z)=\beta(z)/\alpha(z)=\wp''(z)/\wp'(z)$. Letting $w\to z$ and using the continuity of $\wp$ near $2z$, of $\wp$ near $z$ and of $Q$ [F6] gives $\wp(2z)=-2\wp(z)+\tfrac14(\wp''(z)/\wp'(z))^2$. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

2.1 (Rational expression in $\wp$ and $\wp'$.) Substituting the identity of step 1.1 into the duplication identity of step 1.2 gives, for every $z\in\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$ with $\wp'(z)\ne0$, $$\wp(2z)=-2\wp(z)+\frac14\left(\frac{6\wp(z)^2-\frac12g_2}{\wp'(z)}\right)^{2}=-2\wp(z)+\frac{(6\wp(z)^2-\frac12g_2)^2}{4\,\wp'(z)^2},$$ a value of the rational function $R(x,y)=-2x+\dfrac{(6x^2-\frac12g_2)^2}{4y^2}$ of the two variables $x,y$ with coefficients in the field generated by $g_2$ over $\mathbb C$ (here the denominator $4y^2$ does not vanish because $\wp'(z)\ne0$). [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 (Meromorphic extension and pole set.) The function $F(z):=\wp(2z)$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb C$: it is holomorphic off $\tfrac12\Lambda=\{z:2z\in\Lambda\}$, and if $z_0\in\tfrac12\Lambda$ with $\lambda:=2z_0\in\Lambda$, then [F1] gives that $\wp(w)-(w-\lambda)^{-2}$ is holomorphic near $\lambda$, so substituting $w=2z$ shows $F(z)-\tfrac14(z-z_0)^{-2}$ holomorphic near $z_0$: each $z_0\in\tfrac12\Lambda$ is a double pole of $F$, and there are no others. The right-hand side $R(\wp(z),\wp'(z))$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb C$ by the field property [F7], because $\wp$ and $\wp'$ are meromorphic and $\wp'$ is not the zero function by [F2]. By steps 1.2 and 2.1 the two meromorphic functions agree on $\{z\in\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda:\wp'(z)\ne0\}=\mathbb C\setminus\tfrac12\Lambda$, a nonempty open subset of the connected domain $\mathbb C$ [F8]; hence their difference vanishes on a nonempty open set and is identically zero by [F7]. Therefore the duplication identity is an identity of meromorphic functions on $\mathbb C$: it holds wherever both sides are finite, and at the points of $\tfrac12\Lambda$, where $F$ has a double pole and the right-hand side likewise has a pole (at half-periods because $\wp'$ has a zero of order one and $\wp''$ is nonzero there, and at lattice points by the equality of the two meromorphic functions), no finite value is asserted. [F1, F2, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 (Assembly.) Step 1.1 gives the identity $\wp''=6\wp^2-\tfrac12g_2$ on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$, extended holomorphically across the half-periods where the division by $\wp'$ was only apparently problematic; step 1.2 gives the duplication identity for $\wp'(z)\ne0$; step 2.1 exhibits it as the rational expression in $\wp(z)$ and $\wp'(z)$; and step 3.1 upgrades the duplication identity to an identity of meromorphic functions on $\mathbb C$, with the genuine poles retained. These are exactly the assertions of the example. ∎

## Remarks

The only point of substance is that the addition formula becomes $0/0$ when
$w=z$: the secant through two coincident points has to be replaced by the
tangent, and in the formula that means replacing the difference quotient by
the derivative quotient $\wp''(z)/\wp'(z)$. The second identity is what makes
the result algebraic: $(\wp')^2=4\wp^3-g_2\wp-g_3$ can be differentiated and
solved for $\wp''$ wherever $\wp'\ne0$, and the apparent failure of that
solution at the half-periods is repaired by the identity theorem, since
$\wp''$ and $6\wp^2-\tfrac12g_2$ are holomorphic across them. Both formulas are
used in [[thm-elliptic-cubic-chord-tangent-group-law]], where the tangent case
of the chord-tangent law is exactly the limiting case $w\to z$ used here; note
that the theorem derives its own copy of the differentiated differential
equation locally, so this example carries no load for it.

## Example

For the coefficient pair $(g_2,g_3)=(3,1)$ the number
$\Delta:=g_2^3-27g_3^2=3^3-27\cdot1^2=0$, and the projective cubic
$$Y^2Z=4X^3-3XZ^2-Z^3$$
has the affine singular point $(x,y)=(-1/2,0)$: the affine equation
$y^2=4x^3-3x-1$ factors as $y^2=(x-1)(2x+1)^2$, and near that point the curve
is the union of the two smooth branches $y=\pm(x+\tfrac12)u(x+\tfrac12)$ meeting
transversally. Consequently no full complex lattice has these invariants, and
this cubic is a degeneration *outside* the lattice family; it cannot be used as
a supplier for any lattice statement.

## Example

Put

$$P(z):=\pi\cot(\pi z)\qquad (z\in\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb Z),\qquad q:=e^{2\pi iz}.$$

Then:

1. the map $z\mapsto q$ induces a bijection $\mathbb C/\mathbb Z\to
   \mathbb C^\ast=\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, and
   $P(z)=\pi i\,(q+1)/(q-1)$ for every $z\in\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb Z$;
2. $P$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb Z$, its poles are exactly the
   integers and they are simple of residue $1$, its period group is exactly
   $\mathbb Z$, its principal part at $0$ is $1/z$, and
   $$-P'(z)=P(z)^2+\pi^2\qquad(z\notin\mathbb Z);$$
3. writing $x=P(z)$ and $y=-P'(z)$, the map $z\mapsto[x:y:1]$ extends at the
   class of $0$ to $[0:1:0]$ and identifies $\mathbb C/\mathbb Z$ bijectively
   with the conic $YZ=X^2+\pi^2Z^2$ minus its two points $[-i\pi:0:1]$ and
   $[i\pi:0:1]$; off the class of $0$ the identification is holomorphic with
   nowhere-vanishing derivative.

This is the rank-one analogue of the double-periodic uniformization of the
companion page: there the period lattice $\Lambda$ has rank two, here the
period group is $\mathbb Z$, and the cubic is replaced by a conic.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the functions $\sin,\cos$ of [[def-complex-trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-functions]], the cotangent $\cot x=\cos x/\sin x$ of [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]], the complex exponential $\exp$ of [[def-complex-exponential]], and the function $P(z)=\pi\cot(\pi z)$ on $\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb Z$.

[F2] $\cot x=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}$ for every $x\ne m\pi$ with $m\in\mathbb Z$ ([[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]]).

## Example

Call a ratio $\tau$ **reduced** when

$$\operatorname{Im}\tau>0,\qquad -\tfrac12<\operatorname{Re}\tau\le\tfrac12,\qquad |\tau|\ge1,\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{Re}\tau\ge0\ \text{whenever}\ |\tau|=1,$$

and let $\mathcal R$ be the set of reduced ratios. Every full complex lattice
$\Lambda$ admits an oriented basis $(\omega_1,\omega_2)$ with
$\tau=\omega_2/\omega_1\in\mathcal R$, this reduced ratio is uniquely determined
by $\Lambda$, and the number of oriented bases of $\Lambda$ realizing it is two
in general, four when $\tau=i$, and six when $\tau=e^{i\pi/3}=\tfrac12+\tfrac{\sqrt3}2i$.
The lattices $\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z$ and $\mathbb Z+\mathbb Ze^{i\pi/3}$ realize
the exceptional ratios $i$ and $e^{i\pi/3}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A full complex lattice $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\omega_1+\mathbb Z\omega_2$
with $\omega_1,\omega_2$ real-linearly independent, and $\tau:=\omega_2/\omega_1$.

[F2] Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique real coordinates $z=a+bi$; $\operatorname{Re}z=a$, $\operatorname{Im}z=b$, $\overline z=a-bi$ and $|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]).

## Example

Call a ratio $\tau$ **reduced** when

$$\operatorname{Im}\tau>0,\qquad -\tfrac12<\operatorname{Re}\tau\le\tfrac12,\qquad |\tau|\ge1,\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{Re}\tau\ge0\ \text{whenever}\ |\tau|=1,$$

and let $\mathcal R$ be the set of reduced ratios. Every full complex lattice
$\Lambda$ admits an oriented basis $(\omega_1,\omega_2)$ with
$\tau=\omega_2/\omega_1\in\mathcal R$, this reduced ratio is uniquely determined
by $\Lambda$, and the number of oriented bases of $\Lambda$ realizing it is two
in general, four when $\tau=i$, and six when $\tau=e^{i\pi/3}=\tfrac12+\tfrac{\sqrt3}2i$.
The lattices $\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z$ and $\mathbb Z+\mathbb Ze^{i\pi/3}$ realize
the exceptional ratios $i$ and $e^{i\pi/3}$.

[F3] For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$: $z\overline z=|z|^2$, $|z|\ge0$, $|z|=0$ exactly when $z=0$, $|zw|=|z|\,|w|$ and $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$; conjugation is an involutive real-field automorphism ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

## Example

Let $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\alpha+\mathbb Z\beta$ with $\alpha>0$ real and
$\beta\in i\mathbb R_{>0}$, put $c_1=\alpha/2$, $c_2=\beta/2$,
$c_3=(\alpha+\beta)/2$ and $e_j=\wp(c_j)$, ordered $e_2<e_3<e_1$. Then
for $z\in\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$, $\wp(z)\in\mathbb R$ exactly when
$\operatorname{Re}z\in(\alpha/2)\mathbb Z$ or
$\operatorname{Im}z\in(b/2)\mathbb Z$. These are the horizontal and vertical
lines through $\tfrac12\Lambda$; their lattice points are poles of $\wp$, not
finite real values. The restriction to a half-period rectangle maps
conformally onto one half-plane. Every inverse branch satisfies
$dz/d\zeta=(4\zeta^3-g_2\zeta-g_3)^{-1/2}$, giving
$$\frac{\alpha}{2}=\int_{e_1}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{4x^3-g_2x-g_3}}=\int_{e_2}^{e_3}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{4x^3-g_2x-g_3}},\qquad \frac{\beta}{2i}=\int_{-\infty}^{e_2}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{g_3+g_2x-4x^3}}=\int_{e_3}^{e_1}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{g_3+g_2x-4x^3}},$$
with positive real square roots. In the corresponding Jacobi example, for
$0<k<1$ put $K(a)=\int_0^1 ds/\sqrt{(1-s^2)(1-a^2s^2)}$, $K=K(k)$ and
$K'=K(\sqrt{1-k^2})$. Then
$I_k(z)=\int_0^z d\zeta/\sqrt{(1-\zeta^2)(1-k^2\zeta^2)}$ maps the upper
half-plane conformally onto the rectangle with vertices $-K,K,K+iK',-K+iK'$,
and its inverse sn extends by reflection to a doubly periodic meromorphic
function with periods $4K$ and $2iK'$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A rectangular lattice $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\alpha+\mathbb Z\beta$ with $\alpha>0$ real and $\beta=ib$, $b>0$, the half-periods $c_1=\alpha/2$, $c_2=\beta/2$, $c_3=(\alpha+\beta)/2$, the values $e_j=\wp(c_j)$, the rectangle $S=\{s\alpha/2+t\beta/2:0\le s,t\le1\}$, and a parameter $0<k<1$.

[F1] $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\alpha+\mathbb Z\beta$ is a full complex lattice with oriented basis, $T_\Lambda=\mathbb C/\Lambda$ its torus, and $\wp=\wp_\Lambda$ is the Weierstrass function $z^{-2}+\sum_{\omega\ne0}((z-\omega)^{-2}-\omega^{-2})$ of the lattice, with derivative $\wp'$; $\wp$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$, even, $\Lambda$-periodic, and at every $\lambda\in\Lambda$ has a double pole with principal part $(z-\lambda)^{-2}$ and no other poles ([[def-complex-lattice-and-complex-torus]], [[def-weierstrass-elliptic-p-function]], [[thm-weierstrass-p-normal-convergence-and-periodicity]]).

[F2] $\wp'$ is odd and $\Lambda$-periodic with poles of order three exactly at the lattice points; $\wp(z)=\wp(w)$ holds if and only if $w\equiv\pm z$ modulo $\Lambda$; and the zeros of $\wp'$ are exactly the $\Lambda$-translates of $c_1,c_2,c_3$, each of order one ([[thm-weierstrass-p-normal-convergence-and-periodicity]], [[lem-weierstrass-p-degree-two-and-half-periods]]).

[F3] $(\wp')^2=4\wp^3-g_2\wp-g_3=4(\wp-e_1)(\wp-e_2)(\wp-e_3)$ with $g_2=60G_4$, $g_3=140G_6$, and $e_1,e_2,e_3$ are the three distinct roots of the cubic ([[thm-weierstrass-p-differential-equation]], [[thm-weierstrass-lattice-discriminant-is-nonzero]]); differentiating the identity gives $2\wp'\wp''=(12\wp^2-g_2)\wp'$, hence $\wp''=6\wp^2-g_2/2$ on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$.

[F4] Complex conjugation is a continuous real-field automorphism, so it commutes with sums, products, quotients and limits of convergent nets of complex numbers ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]); $z$ is real exactly when $z=\overline z$, and $\operatorname{Re}z=(z+\overline z)/2$, $\operatorname{Im}z=(z-\overline z)/(2i)$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[thm-complex-numbers-are-the-real-coordinate-plane]]).

[F5] Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has a unique representation $z=s\alpha+t\beta$ with $s,t\in\mathbb R$; subtracting integer parts ([[lem-integer-part]]) gives representatives in $S$ ([[def-complex-lattice-and-complex-torus]], [[thm-complex-numbers-are-the-real-coordinate-plane]]).

[F6] Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, $f$ meromorphic on $\Omega$ and $\Gamma$ admissible for the residue theorem in $\Omega$ with $f\ne0$ on $\Gamma^*$. Then $\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma f'/f=Z(f,\Gamma)-P(f,\Gamma)$, and for $w$ with $f\ne w$ on $\Gamma^*$ the weighted count of preimages of $w$ equals $\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma f'/(f-w)$ ([[thm-argument-principle-null-homologous-cycle]], [[cor-argument-principle-counts-preimages]]); the winding number $n(\gamma,p)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\gamma d\zeta/(\zeta-p)$ of a closed contour about a point off its trace obeys $n(\gamma,p)=Z(\mathrm{id}-p,\gamma)$ ([[def-winding-number-closed-complex-contour]]).

[F7] If a function holomorphic on a half-disc is continuous up to the diameter and real-valued on the open diameter, then it extends holomorphically across the diameter by reflection in the real axis; the same statement holds after composing with a biholomorphism taking a half-disc to a half-disc, and it holds in the meromorphic sense at an isolated boundary pole with real values elsewhere on the boundary ([[thm-harmonic-and-holomorphic-schwarz-reflection-principles]]).

[F8] The upper half-plane $H$ is a complex domain; its complement in $\widehat{\mathbb C}$ is $\{\operatorname{Im}z\le0\}\cup\{\infty\}$, the closure in the sphere of the convex set $\{\operatorname{Im}z\le0\}$. That convex set is contractible, hence path-connected, hence connected ([[cor-convex-subsets-of-rn-are-contractible]], [[cor-contractible-spaces-are-path-connected]], [[thm-path-connected-implies-connected]]), and the closure of a connected set is connected, so $\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus H$ is connected ([[thm-closure-of-a-connected-set]], [[def-complex-domain]]). A complex domain whose complement in $\widehat{\mathbb C}$ is connected has every cycle null-homologous in it, i.e. is homologically simply connected ([[lem-connected-spherical-complement-implies-null-homology]], [[def-homologically-simply-connected-complex-domain]]); on such a domain every holomorphic function has a primitive, and every nowhere-zero holomorphic function has a holomorphic square root ([[thm-homological-simple-connectivity-equivalences]], [[cor-holomorphic-roots-homologically-simply-connected-domains]]).

[F9] If $g$ is continuous on an interval and nowhere zero, then $g$ has constant sign there ([[thm-intermediate-value]]); a positive continuous integrand on an interval gives a strictly increasing integral, and improper integrals at a finite endpoint and at infinity converge or diverge as evaluated there ([[def-improper-integral-at-a-finite-endpoint]], [[def-improper-integral-at-infinity]]); the change-of-variables formula holds for such integrals with the absolute derivative ([[cor-one-dimensional-change-of-variables-with-absolute-derivative]]).

[F10] An injective holomorphic map on a complex domain is biholomorphic onto its open image, with nowhere-zero derivative ([[cor-injective-holomorphic-derivative-nonzero]]).

## Verification

1.1 (Conjugation symmetry of $\wp$ and $\wp'$.) Since $\overline\alpha=\alpha\in\Lambda$ and $\overline\beta=-\beta\in\Lambda$, the lattice is conjugation-invariant. Conjugating the defining net of $\wp$ termwise for $z\notin\Lambda$ and using continuity of conjugation and the local uniform convergence of the net ([F1, F4]) gives $\wp(\overline z)=\overline{\wp(z)}$; differentiating this identity gives $\wp'(\overline z)=\overline{\wp'(z)}$. In particular $\wp$ is real on the real axis, and for $z=x+\beta/2$ one has $\overline z=z-\beta\equiv z$ modulo $\Lambda$, so $\wp(\overline z)=\wp(z)$ and $\wp(z)=\overline{\wp(z)}$: $\wp$ is real on the two lines $\operatorname{Im}z=0$ and $\operatorname{Im}z=b/2$. [F1, F4, F5]

1.2 (The half-period rectangle: no poles and no critical points inside.) Put $S=\{s\tfrac\alpha2+t\tfrac\beta2:0\le s,t\le1\}$; its interior $S^\circ$ is $\{0<s,t<1\}$ in these coordinates. An interior point $z=s\alpha/2+t\beta/2$ is not in $\Lambda$: if $z=m\alpha+n\beta$ with $m,n\in\mathbb Z$, then $s=2m$ and $t=2n$ by uniqueness of coordinates ([F5]), but $0<s,t<1$ excludes integers. It is not a zero of $\wp'$: such a zero would satisfy $z\equiv c_j$ modulo $\Lambda$ ([F2]) for one of $c_1=\alpha/2$, $c_2=\beta/2$, $c_3=(\alpha+\beta)/2$, i.e. $(s,t)$ would differ from $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$ by even integers, forcing $s\in 2\mathbb Z+1$ or $t\in 2\mathbb Z+1$, again impossible for $0<s,t<1$. Consequently $\wp$ is holomorphic on $S^\circ$, $\wp'\ne0$ there, and for $z,w\in S^\circ$ the equality $\wp(z)=\wp(w)$ forces $w\equiv\pm z$ by [F2]: a lattice shift $w=z+\lambda$ forces $s'-s,t'-t\in2\mathbb Z$ with $|s'-s|<1$, hence $s=s'$, $t=t'$; and a sign choice $w=-z+\lambda$ forces $s+s'\in2\mathbb Z$ with $0<s+s'<2$, hence $s+s'=2$ (impossible, as $s,s'<1$) or $s+s'=0$ (impossible). Thus $\wp$ is injective on $S^\circ$. [F1, F2, F5]

1.3 (The Jacobi integrand: a normalized square root on $H$.) Let $H=\{z:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$ and $P(\zeta)=(1-\zeta^2)(1-k^2\zeta^2)$. Its zeros are $\pm1,\pm1/k$, all real, so $P$ is holomorphic and nowhere zero on the simply connected domain $H$; by [F8] there is a holomorphic square root $q$ of $P$ on $H$. On $(-1,1)$ the function $q^2=P$ is positive, so $q$ is continuous and nowhere zero there with $q(x)=\pm\sqrt{P(x)}$: the sign is constant by [F9], and after replacing $q$ by $-q$ if necessary we may and do assume $q(x)>0$ for $-1<x<1$. Then $1/q$ is holomorphic on $H$ and, by [F8], has a primitive $I_k(z)=\int_0^z d\zeta/q(\zeta)$ normalized by $I_k(0)=0$; it satisfies $I_k'(z)=1/q(z)\ne0$ on $H$. [F8, F9]

2.1 (The exact real locus.) For $z\in\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$: $\wp(z)\in\mathbb R$ iff $\wp(z)=\overline{\wp(z)}=\wp(\overline z)$ iff $\overline z\equiv\pm z$ modulo $\Lambda$ by the fibre criterion ([F2]); and $\overline z\equiv z$ means $2i\operatorname{Im}z\in\Lambda$, i.e. $\operatorname{Im}z\in\tfrac b2\mathbb Z$, while $\overline z\equiv-z$ means $2\operatorname{Re}z\in\Lambda$, i.e. $\operatorname{Re}z\in\tfrac\alpha2\mathbb Z$ ([F4, F5]). Thus on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$ the real-value locus is exactly the union of the horizontal lines $\operatorname{Im}z\in\tfrac b2\mathbb Z$ and the vertical lines $\operatorname{Re}z\in\tfrac\alpha2\mathbb Z$; the excluded lattice points on those lines are poles by [F1]. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1]

2.2 (Monotonicity along the four edges and the order $e_2<e_3<e_1$.) The boundary $\partial S$ consists of the images of the four segments $0\to c_1\to c_3\to c_2\to0$. On the open segment from $0$ to $c_1$ (a real interval), $\wp$ is real (step 1.1), has no pole and no critical point, so its derivative is continuous and nowhere zero, hence of constant sign ([F9]); since $\wp(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to0^+$ by the principal part in [F1] and $\wp(c_1)=e_1$, this sign is negative and $\wp$ decreases strictly from $+\infty$ to $e_1$. Likewise along the open segment from $c_1$ to $c_3$ and from $c_3$ to $c_2$ and from $c_2$ to $0$, all lying on the real locus lines, $\wp$ takes real values with nowhere-zero derivative and is thus strictly monotone; the segment from $c_2$ to $0$ is the imaginary interval because $c_2=ib/2$, and $\wp(iy)\to-\infty$ as $y\to0^+$ by [F1], so there $\wp$ decreases to $-\infty$. Because $\wp'(c_j)=0$ ([F2]), Taylor expansion at $c_j$ using [F3] gives $\wp(c_j+w)=e_j+\tfrac12\wp''(c_j)w^2+O(|w|^3)$ with $\wp''(c_j)=6e_j^2-g_2/2$ and, comparing the expansions of both sides of $(\wp')^2=4(\wp-e_1)(\wp-e_2)(\wp-e_3)$, $\wp''(c_j)=2\prod_{i\ne j}(e_j-e_i)$. At $c_1$ the incident edge towards $0$ has values $>e_1$ and the incident edge towards $c_3$ has values $<e_1$ (both signs by the second-order expansion, whose quadratic coefficient for the first edge is $+\wp''(c_1)/2$ and for the second $-\wp''(c_1)/2$), so $e_3<e_1$. At $c_2$ the incident edge towards $0$ has values $<e_2$ and the incident edge towards $c_3$ has values $>e_2$, so $e_3>e_2$. Hence $e_2<e_3<e_1$. [F1, F2, F3, F9, step 1.1]

2.3 (Boundary values of $q$ and $I_k$.) The function $q$ is continuous on $H\cup(\mathbb R\setminus\{\pm1,\pm1/k\})$, because $q^2=P$ and $q\ne0$ near every such boundary point. On each of the intervals cut out by the zeros, the boundary value $q(x+i0)$ is a continuous square root of the real number $P(x)$, hence equals $\pm\sqrt{P(x)}$ or $\pm i\sqrt{|P(x)|}$ with a sign that is constant on the interval ([F9]). The signs are computed at the zeros: at $z=1$, write $P(z)=(z-1)g(z)$ with $g(1)=P'(1)=-2(1-k^2)<0$; for $z=1+re^{i\theta}$, $0\le\theta\le\pi$, the quantity $A(\theta)=q(z)r^{-1/2}e^{-i\theta/2}$ is continuous in $\theta$ and $A(\theta)^2=P(z)/(z-1)\to P'(1)<0$ uniformly, so $A$ is constantly $\pm i\sqrt{|P'(1)|}$; at $\theta=\pi$ one has $z=1-r$ and $q(z)=\sqrt{P(1-r)}=A(\pi)\sqrt r\,e^{i\pi/2}$, so $A(\pi)=-i\sqrt{|P'(1)|}$ and therefore $q(1+re^{i\theta})\to -i\sqrt{|P(1+r)|}$ as $\theta\downarrow0$; by constancy of sign, $q(x+i0)=-i\sqrt{(x^2-1)(1-k^2x^2)}$ for $1<x<1/k$. The same computation at $z=-1$ (where $q(-1+r)=\sqrt{P(-1+r)}>0$ and $P'(-1)=2(1-k^2)>0$) gives $q(x+i0)=+i\sqrt{(x^2-1)(1-k^2x^2)}$ for $-1/k<x<-1$. At $z=1/k$ and $z=-1/k$ one has $P'(1/k)=2(1-k^2)/k>0$ and $P'(-1/k)=-2(1-k^2)/k<0$; applying the same continuous-argument computation at $z=1/k$, starting from the known value $q=-i\sqrt{|P|}$ on $(1,1/k)$, gives $q(x+i0)=-\sqrt{P(x)}$ for $x>1/k$, and applying it at $z=-1/k$, starting from the known value $q=+i\sqrt{|P|}$ on $(-1/k,-1)$, gives $q(x+i0)=-\sqrt{P(x)}$ for $x<-1/k$. Hence, using $I_k'(x+i0)=1/q(x+i0)$ and $I_k(0)=0$: $I_k$ is strictly increasing on $(-1,1)$ with $I_k(\pm1)=\pm K$; $I_k(x)=K+i\int_1^x ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(1-k^2s^2)}$ for $1\le x\le 1/k$, so $I_k(1/k)=K+iK'(k)$ where $K'(k)=\int_1^{1/k}ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(1-k^2s^2)}$; $I_k(x)=-K+i\int_x^{-1}ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(1-k^2s^2)}$ for $-1/k\le x\le-1$, so $I_k(-1/k)=-K+iK'(k)$; and on the tails $I_k(x)=I_k(1/k)-\int_{1/k}^x ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(k^2s^2-1)}$ and $I_k(x)=I_k(-1/k)+\int_x^{-1/k}ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(k^2s^2-1)}$, with $\int_{1/k}^{\infty}ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(k^2s^2-1)}=K$ and $\int_{-\infty}^{-1/k}ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(k^2s^2-1)}=K$, so both tails tend to $iK'(k)$. Here $\int_1^{1/k}ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(1-k^2s^2)}=K(\sqrt{1-k^2})=K'$ under the substitution $s=(1-k'^2u^2)^{-1/2}$ with $k'=\sqrt{1-k^2}$, and $\int_{1/k}^{\infty}ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(k^2s^2-1)}=K$ under $s=1/(ku)$, both by the change-of-variables formula ([F9]). Finally, for $|z|=R>1/k$ in $H$ one has $|P(z)|\ge(R^2-1)(k^2R^2-1)$, so the integral of $1/q$ along the semicircle of radius $R$ is $O(1/R)$; since $I_k(R)\to iK'(k)$ along the real axis, $I_k(z)\to iK'(k)$ uniformly as $|z|\to\infty$ in $H$. [F4, F8, F9, step 1.3]

3.1 (The image lies in one half-plane.) $S^\circ$ is convex, hence connected, and $\wp(S^\circ)$ is connected; since $\wp'\ne0$ on $S^\circ$, $\wp$ is an open map there and $\wp(S^\circ)$ is open ([F10]); and $\wp(S^\circ)\cap\mathbb R=\varnothing$ by step 2.1, because no interior point lies on any of the lines $\operatorname{Re}z\in\tfrac\alpha2\mathbb Z$, $\operatorname{Im}z\in\tfrac b2\mathbb Z$. An open connected subset of $\mathbb C\setminus(\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\})$ is contained in the upper or in the lower half-plane. [F4, step 2.1, step 1.2]

3.2 (The boundary maps onto $\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$.) By step 2.2 the four open edges have images $(e_1,\infty)$, the interval between $e_1$ and $e_3$, the interval between $e_3$ and $e_2$, and $(-\infty,e_2)$, and with $e_2<e_3<e_1$ these intervals are $(e_1,\infty)$, $(e_3,e_1)$, $(e_2,e_3)$ and $(-\infty,e_2)$, which together with the endpoint values and $\wp(0)=\infty$ cover $\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$ exactly once on the boundary circle. [F1, step 2.2]

3.3 ($I_k$ maps $H$ biholomorphically onto the interior of the rectangle.) Let $R_0$ be the open rectangle $( -K,K)\times(0,K')$ with $K'=K'(k)=K(\sqrt{1-k^2})$, and for $R>1/k$ let $D_R=\{z\in H:|z|<R\}$, whose boundary is the segment $[-R,R]$ followed by the semicircle. By step 2.3 the image of $[-R,R]$ under $I_k$ is a closed curve that follows $\partial R_0$ once in the counterclockwise sense (from a point near $iK'$ along the top-left, down, around, and back along the top-right to a point near $iK'$), while the image of the semicircle lies in the disc of radius $O(1/R)$ about $iK'$. Fix $w\in R_0$ and take $R$ so large that $O(1/R)<\operatorname{dist}(w,iK')$ and $w$ is not on the image of $\partial D_R$ (the real-axis image is contained in $\partial R_0$, which does not contain $w$; the semicircle image misses $w$ by the distance bound). Then $I_k-w$ has no zeros on $\partial D_R$, and by the argument principle [F6] the number of zeros of $I_k-w$ in $D_R$ (each simple, because $I_k'\ne0$) equals the winding number about $w$ of the closed curve $I_k(\partial D_R)$, namely the sum of the winding number $1$ of the $\partial R_0$-loop and the winding number $0$ of the small semicircle image, hence equals $1$. Taking $R\to\infty$ (the count is eventually constant, and every zero of $I_k-w$ lies in a bounded set because $I_k(z)\to iK'\ne w$ as $|z|\to\infty$) shows that $w$ is attained exactly once in $H$. If $w\in\mathbb C\setminus\overline{R_0}$ with $w\ne iK'$ then the same computation gives winding number $0$ and (taking $R$ large with $w$ off the curve) no preimage; if $w\in\partial R_0\setminus\{iK'\}$ had a preimage $z_0\in H$, then $I_k(H)$ would be a neighbourhood of $w$ containing points outside $\overline{R_0}$, contradicting the preceding sentence; and the same openness argument excludes a preimage of $iK'$, since $I_k(z)\to iK'$ and no point above the top edge is attained. Therefore $I_k(H)=R_0$, and the injective holomorphic $I_k:H\to R_0$ is biholomorphic by [F10]. [F6, F10, step 2.3]

4.1 (The image of $S$ is exactly one half-plane and $\wp|_S$ is conformal.) Every boundary point of $\wp(S^\circ)$ is a limit $\wp(z_n)$ with $z_n\in S^\circ$; by compactness of $\overline S$ pass to a subsequence with $z_n\to z_0\in\overline S$ and $\wp(z_0)=w$ with the value $\wp(0)=\infty$ allowed. If $z_0\in S^\circ$ then $w\in\wp(S^\circ)$, which is impossible for a boundary point because $\wp(S^\circ)$ is open; hence $z_0\in\partial S$ and, by step 3.2, $w\in\wp(\partial S)\subseteq\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$. Thus $\partial\wp(S^\circ)\subseteq\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$, while by step 3.1 the set $\wp(S^\circ)$ is a nonempty open connected subset of one half-plane $U_\pm$, and $U_\pm\cap(\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\})=\varnothing$. If $w\in U_\pm\setminus\wp(S^\circ)$, join $w$ to a point $q\in\wp(S^\circ)$ by the segment $\gamma$ inside the convex set $U_\pm$ and let $t_0=\inf\{t:\gamma(t)\in\wp(S^\circ)\}$; then $\gamma(t_0)\in\partial\wp(S^\circ)\cap U_\pm$, contradicting $\partial\wp(S^\circ)\subseteq\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$. Hence $\wp(S^\circ)=U_\pm$, and $\wp:S^\circ\to U_\pm$ is injective with nowhere-zero derivative, hence biholomorphic, and in particular conformal. [F10, step 3.1, step 3.2]

5.1 (Derivative of the inverse branch.) Let $U=U_\pm$ and $f=\wp|_{S^\circ}^{-1}:U\to S^\circ$. Then $f$ is holomorphic, $\wp(f(\zeta))=\zeta$ for $\zeta\in U$, and the chain rule gives $\wp'(f(\zeta))f'(\zeta)=1$, so $f'(\zeta)=1/\wp'(f(\zeta))$. Substituting $\wp(f(\zeta))=\zeta$ in the differential equation [F3] gives $\wp'(f(\zeta))^2=4\zeta^3-g_2\zeta-g_3$, and since $f'$ is nowhere zero its reciprocal $\zeta\mapsto 1/f'(\zeta)=\wp'(f(\zeta))$ is a holomorphic square root of $4\zeta^3-g_2\zeta-g_3$ on $U$; writing $(4\zeta^3-g_2\zeta-g_3)^{-1/2}$ for that reciprocal root, every inverse branch satisfies $f'(\zeta)=(4\zeta^3-g_2\zeta-g_3)^{-1/2}$. [F3, step 4.1]

6.1 (The four period integrals.) On each of the four real intervals between consecutive roots the polynomial $4x^3-g_2x-g_3=4(x-e_1)(x-e_2)(x-e_3)$ has constant sign; $4x^3-g_2x-g_3>0$ on $(e_1,\infty)$ and on $(e_2,e_3)$, while $g_3+g_2x-4x^3>0$ on $(-\infty,e_2)$ and on $(e_3,e_1)$. Each of these intervals is the image under $\wp$ of one open edge of $\partial S$, and the inverse branch $f$ maps it bijectively onto that edge with $|f'(x)|=1/\sqrt{|4x^3-g_2x-g_3|}$ by step 5.1, so the integral of the positive square root over the interval equals the length of the corresponding displacement: writing the inverse branch as $g$, $\int_a^b dx/\sqrt{|4x^3-g_2x-g_3|}=|\lim_{x\downarrow a}g(x)-\lim_{x\uparrow b}g(x)|$ by the change-of-variables formula and strict monotonicity of $g$ ([F9]). The four displacements are: from $0$ to $c_1$, length $\alpha/2$; from $c_2$ to $c_3$, length $\alpha/2$; from $c_2$ to $0$, length $|\beta|/2=\beta/(2i)$; from $c_1$ to $c_3$, length $\beta/(2i)$. Hence the four displayed identities hold with the positive real square roots. [F1, F2, F3, F9, step 2.2, step 3.2, step 5.1]

7.1 (The inverse sn and its double periodicity.) Let $\mathrm{sn}=I_k^{-1}:R_0\to H$; it is holomorphic ([F10]) and continuous on $\overline{R_0}\setminus\{iK'\}$ with real boundary values: the bottom edge $[-K,K]$ maps into $(-1,1)$ with $\mathrm{sn}(0)=0$, $\mathrm{sn}(\pm K)=\pm1$; the left edge $-K+i(0,K')$ maps into $(-1/k,-1)$ with $\mathrm{sn}(-K+iK')=-1/k$ (by the continuation across the pole at $-1/k$); the right edge $K+i(0,K')$ maps into $(1,1/k)$ with $\mathrm{sn}(K+iK')=1/k$; and the top edge $(-K,K)+iK'$ maps into $\mathbb R$ with $|\mathrm{sn}|>1/k$, with a simple pole at $iK'$ (from step 2.3, $I_k(z)=iK'+1/(kz)+O(z^{-2})$ for large $z$, so near the omitted value $iK'$ the inverse behaves like $1/(k(w-iK'))$). Since $\mathrm{sn}$ is holomorphic on $R_0$ and real on each of the four open sides, the Schwarz reflection principle [F7] extends it across each side by reflection there: away from $iK'$ this is the stated holomorphic reflection, and at $iK'$ one applies the same principle to the reciprocal $u=1/\mathrm{sn}$, which is holomorphic near $iK'$ with $u(iK')=0$ and real boundary values, so $u$ reflects and $\mathrm{sn}=1/u$ reflects meromorphically; the reflected copies tile the plane, because the four reflections $\sigma_b(z)=\overline z$, $\sigma_t(z)=\overline z+2iK'$, $\sigma_l(z)=-2K-\overline z$, $\sigma_r(z)=2K-\overline z$ generate the group generated by the translations $\sigma_b\sigma_t:z\mapsto z-2iK'$ and $\sigma_r\sigma_l:z\mapsto z+4K$, whose orbits of the rectangle tile the plane. The resulting single meromorphic function $\mathrm{sn}$ on $\mathbb C$ satisfies $\mathrm{sn}(\sigma_jz)=\overline{\mathrm{sn}(z)}$ for each reflection $\sigma_j$, so $\mathrm{sn}(z-2iK')=\overline{\mathrm{sn}(\sigma_tz)}=\mathrm{sn}(z)$ and $\mathrm{sn}(z+4K)=\overline{\mathrm{sn}(\sigma_lz)}=\mathrm{sn}(z)$: $\mathrm{sn}$ is doubly periodic with periods $4K$ and $2iK'$ (and period $2iK'$ implies period $-2iK'$). ∎

## Remarks

The sign analysis is the only delicate point. The normalized square root $q$ of $(1-\zeta^2)(1-k^2\zeta^2)$ is positive on $(-1,1)$, and the local factorizations at $\pm1$ and $\pm1/k$ force the boundary values $-i\sqrt{|P|}$ on $(1,1/k)$, $+i\sqrt{|P|}$ on $(-1/k,-1)$, and $-\sqrt{P}$ on both tails; the two tails then approach the same point $iK'$, which is what closes the image of the real axis into the boundary of the rectangle. The same computation for $\wp$ gives $e_2<e_3<e_1$ directly from the second-order expansions at $c_1$ and $c_2$; no numerical evaluation of any elliptic integral is used, only the two standard substitutions reducing $K'(k)$ to $K(\sqrt{1-k^2})$ and the tail integral to $K$ itself.

## Example

Let $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\alpha+\mathbb Z\beta$ with $\alpha>0$ real and
$\beta\in i\mathbb R_{>0}$, put $c_1=\alpha/2$, $c_2=\beta/2$,
$c_3=(\alpha+\beta)/2$ and $e_j=\wp(c_j)$, ordered $e_2<e_3<e_1$. Then
for $z\in\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$, $\wp(z)\in\mathbb R$ exactly when
$\operatorname{Re}z\in(\alpha/2)\mathbb Z$ or
$\operatorname{Im}z\in(b/2)\mathbb Z$. These are the horizontal and vertical
lines through $\tfrac12\Lambda$; their lattice points are poles of $\wp$, not
finite real values. The restriction to a half-period rectangle maps
conformally onto one half-plane. Every inverse branch satisfies
$dz/d\zeta=(4\zeta^3-g_2\zeta-g_3)^{-1/2}$, giving
$$\frac{\alpha}{2}=\int_{e_1}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{4x^3-g_2x-g_3}}=\int_{e_2}^{e_3}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{4x^3-g_2x-g_3}},\qquad \frac{\beta}{2i}=\int_{-\infty}^{e_2}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{g_3+g_2x-4x^3}}=\int_{e_3}^{e_1}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{g_3+g_2x-4x^3}},$$
with positive real square roots. In the corresponding Jacobi example, for
$0<k<1$ put $K(a)=\int_0^1 ds/\sqrt{(1-s^2)(1-a^2s^2)}$, $K=K(k)$ and
$K'=K(\sqrt{1-k^2})$. Then
$I_k(z)=\int_0^z d\zeta/\sqrt{(1-\zeta^2)(1-k^2\zeta^2)}$ maps the upper
half-plane conformally onto the rectangle with vertices $-K,K,K+iK',-K+iK'$,
and its inverse sn extends by reflection to a doubly periodic meromorphic
function with periods $4K$ and $2iK'$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A rectangular lattice $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\alpha+\mathbb Z\beta$ with $\alpha>0$ real and $\beta=ib$, $b>0$, the half-periods $c_1=\alpha/2$, $c_2=\beta/2$, $c_3=(\alpha+\beta)/2$, the values $e_j=\wp(c_j)$, the rectangle $S=\{s\alpha/2+t\beta/2:0\le s,t\le1\}$, and a parameter $0<k<1$.

[F1] $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\alpha+\mathbb Z\beta$ is a full complex lattice with oriented basis, $T_\Lambda=\mathbb C/\Lambda$ its torus, and $\wp=\wp_\Lambda$ is the Weierstrass function $z^{-2}+\sum_{\omega\ne0}((z-\omega)^{-2}-\omega^{-2})$ of the lattice, with derivative $\wp'$; $\wp$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$, even, $\Lambda$-periodic, and at every $\lambda\in\Lambda$ has a double pole with principal part $(z-\lambda)^{-2}$ and no other poles ([[def-complex-lattice-and-complex-torus]], [[def-weierstrass-elliptic-p-function]], [[thm-weierstrass-p-normal-convergence-and-periodicity]]).

[F2] $\wp'$ is odd and $\Lambda$-periodic with poles of order three exactly at the lattice points; $\wp(z)=\wp(w)$ holds if and only if $w\equiv\pm z$ modulo $\Lambda$; and the zeros of $\wp'$ are exactly the $\Lambda$-translates of $c_1,c_2,c_3$, each of order one ([[thm-weierstrass-p-normal-convergence-and-periodicity]], [[lem-weierstrass-p-degree-two-and-half-periods]]).

[F3] $(\wp')^2=4\wp^3-g_2\wp-g_3=4(\wp-e_1)(\wp-e_2)(\wp-e_3)$ with $g_2=60G_4$, $g_3=140G_6$, and $e_1,e_2,e_3$ are the three distinct roots of the cubic ([[thm-weierstrass-p-differential-equation]], [[thm-weierstrass-lattice-discriminant-is-nonzero]]); differentiating the identity gives $2\wp'\wp''=(12\wp^2-g_2)\wp'$, hence $\wp''=6\wp^2-g_2/2$ on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$.

[F4] Complex conjugation is a continuous real-field automorphism, so it commutes with sums, products, quotients and limits of convergent nets of complex numbers ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]); $z$ is real exactly when $z=\overline z$, and $\operatorname{Re}z=(z+\overline z)/2$, $\operatorname{Im}z=(z-\overline z)/(2i)$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[thm-complex-numbers-are-the-real-coordinate-plane]]).

[F5] Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has a unique representation $z=s\alpha+t\beta$ with $s,t\in\mathbb R$; subtracting integer parts ([[lem-integer-part]]) gives representatives in $S$ ([[def-complex-lattice-and-complex-torus]], [[thm-complex-numbers-are-the-real-coordinate-plane]]).

[F6] Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, $f$ meromorphic on $\Omega$ and $\Gamma$ admissible for the residue theorem in $\Omega$ with $f\ne0$ on $\Gamma^*$. Then $\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma f'/f=Z(f,\Gamma)-P(f,\Gamma)$, and for $w$ with $f\ne w$ on $\Gamma^*$ the weighted count of preimages of $w$ equals $\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma f'/(f-w)$ ([[thm-argument-principle-null-homologous-cycle]], [[cor-argument-principle-counts-preimages]]); the winding number $n(\gamma,p)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\gamma d\zeta/(\zeta-p)$ of a closed contour about a point off its trace obeys $n(\gamma,p)=Z(\mathrm{id}-p,\gamma)$ ([[def-winding-number-closed-complex-contour]]). For a holomorphic map near a closed contour the argument-principle integral equals the winding number of its image ([[thm-argument-principle-as-image-winding-number]]). Winding numbers are invariant under a homotopy of closed rectifiable loops avoiding $p$: apply homotopy invariance of the integral of $1/(z-p)$, joining moving basepoints to the original basepoint and cancelling the joining paths ([[thm-homotopy-invariance-of-holomorphic-line-integrals]]).

[F7] If a function holomorphic on a half-disc is continuous up to the diameter and real-valued on the open diameter, then it extends holomorphically across the diameter by reflection in the real axis; the same statement holds after composing with a biholomorphism taking a half-disc to a half-disc, and it holds in the meromorphic sense at an isolated boundary pole with real values elsewhere on the boundary ([[thm-harmonic-and-holomorphic-schwarz-reflection-principles]]).

[F8] The upper half-plane $H$ is a complex domain; its complement in $\widehat{\mathbb C}$ is $\{\operatorname{Im}z\le0\}\cup\{\infty\}$, the closure in the sphere of the convex set $\{\operatorname{Im}z\le0\}$. That convex set is contractible, hence path-connected, hence connected ([[cor-convex-subsets-of-rn-are-contractible]], [[cor-contractible-spaces-are-path-connected]], [[thm-path-connected-implies-connected]]), and the closure of a connected set is connected, so $\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus H$ is connected ([[thm-closure-of-a-connected-set]], [[def-complex-domain]]). A complex domain whose complement in $\widehat{\mathbb C}$ is connected has every cycle null-homologous in it, i.e. is homologically simply connected ([[lem-connected-spherical-complement-implies-null-homology]], [[def-homologically-simply-connected-complex-domain]]); on such a domain every holomorphic function has a primitive, and every nowhere-zero holomorphic function has a holomorphic square root ([[thm-homological-simple-connectivity-equivalences]], [[cor-holomorphic-roots-homologically-simply-connected-domains]]).

[F9] If $g$ is continuous on an interval and nowhere zero, then $g$ has constant sign there ([[thm-intermediate-value]]); a positive continuous integrand on an interval gives a strictly increasing integral, and improper integrals at a finite endpoint and at infinity converge or diverge as evaluated there ([[def-improper-integral-at-a-finite-endpoint]], [[def-improper-integral-at-infinity]]); the change-of-variables formula holds for such integrals with the absolute derivative ([[cor-one-dimensional-change-of-variables-with-absolute-derivative]]).

[F10] An injective holomorphic map on a complex domain is biholomorphic onto its open image, with nowhere-zero derivative ([[cor-injective-holomorphic-derivative-nonzero]]).

## Verification

1.1 (Conjugation symmetry of $\wp$ and $\wp'$.) Since $\overline\alpha=\alpha\in\Lambda$ and $\overline\beta=-\beta\in\Lambda$, the lattice is conjugation-invariant. Conjugating the defining net of $\wp$ termwise for $z\notin\Lambda$ and using continuity of conjugation and the local uniform convergence of the net ([F1, F4]) gives $\wp(\overline z)=\overline{\wp(z)}$; differentiating this identity gives $\wp'(\overline z)=\overline{\wp'(z)}$. In particular $\wp$ is real on the real axis, and for $z=x+\beta/2$ one has $\overline z=z-\beta\equiv z$ modulo $\Lambda$, so $\wp(\overline z)=\wp(z)$ and $\wp(z)=\overline{\wp(z)}$: $\wp$ is real on the two lines $\operatorname{Im}z=0$ and $\operatorname{Im}z=b/2$. [F1, F4, F5]

1.2 (The half-period rectangle: no poles and no critical points inside.) Put $S=\{s\tfrac\alpha2+t\tfrac\beta2:0\le s,t\le1\}$; its interior $S^\circ$ is $\{0<s,t<1\}$ in these coordinates. An interior point $z=s\alpha/2+t\beta/2$ is not in $\Lambda$: if $z=m\alpha+n\beta$ with $m,n\in\mathbb Z$, then $s=2m$ and $t=2n$ by uniqueness of coordinates ([F5]), but $0<s,t<1$ excludes integers. It is not a zero of $\wp'$: such a zero would satisfy $z\equiv c_j$ modulo $\Lambda$ ([F2]) for one of $c_1=\alpha/2$, $c_2=\beta/2$, $c_3=(\alpha+\beta)/2$, i.e. $(s,t)$ would differ from $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$ by even integers, forcing $s\in 2\mathbb Z+1$ or $t\in 2\mathbb Z+1$, again impossible for $0<s,t<1$. Consequently $\wp$ is holomorphic on $S^\circ$, $\wp'\ne0$ there, and for $z,w\in S^\circ$ the equality $\wp(z)=\wp(w)$ forces $w\equiv\pm z$ by [F2]: a lattice shift $w=z+\lambda$ forces $s'-s,t'-t\in2\mathbb Z$ with $|s'-s|<1$, hence $s=s'$, $t=t'$; and a sign choice $w=-z+\lambda$ forces $s+s'\in2\mathbb Z$ with $0<s+s'<2$, hence $s+s'=2$ (impossible, as $s,s'<1$) or $s+s'=0$ (impossible). Thus $\wp$ is injective on $S^\circ$. [F1, F2, F5]

1.3 (The Jacobi integrand: a normalized square root on $H$.) Let $H=\{z:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$ and $P(\zeta)=(1-\zeta^2)(1-k^2\zeta^2)$. Its zeros are $\pm1,\pm1/k$, all real, so $P$ is holomorphic and nowhere zero on the simply connected domain $H$; by [F8] there is a holomorphic square root $q$ of $P$ on $H$. On $(-1,1)$ the function $q^2=P$ is positive, so $q$ is continuous and nowhere zero there with $q(x)=\pm\sqrt{P(x)}$: the sign is constant by [F9], and after replacing $q$ by $-q$ if necessary we may and do assume $q(x)>0$ for $-1<x<1$. Then $1/q$ is holomorphic on $H$ and, by [F8], has a primitive $I_k(z)=\int_0^z d\zeta/q(\zeta)$ normalized by $I_k(0)=0$; it satisfies $I_k'(z)=1/q(z)\ne0$ on $H$. [F8, F9]

2.1 (The exact real locus.) For $z\in\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$: $\wp(z)\in\mathbb R$ iff $\wp(z)=\overline{\wp(z)}=\wp(\overline z)$ iff $\overline z\equiv\pm z$ modulo $\Lambda$ by the fibre criterion ([F2]); and $\overline z\equiv z$ means $2i\operatorname{Im}z\in\Lambda$, i.e. $\operatorname{Im}z\in\tfrac b2\mathbb Z$, while $\overline z\equiv-z$ means $2\operatorname{Re}z\in\Lambda$, i.e. $\operatorname{Re}z\in\tfrac\alpha2\mathbb Z$ ([F4, F5]). Thus on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$ the real-value locus is exactly the union of the horizontal lines $\operatorname{Im}z\in\tfrac b2\mathbb Z$ and the vertical lines $\operatorname{Re}z\in\tfrac\alpha2\mathbb Z$; the excluded lattice points on those lines are poles by [F1]. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1]

2.2 (Monotonicity along the four edges and the order $e_2<e_3<e_1$.) The boundary $\partial S$ consists of the images of the four segments $0\to c_1\to c_3\to c_2\to0$. On the open segment from $0$ to $c_1$ (a real interval), $\wp$ is real (step 1.1), has no pole and no critical point, so its derivative is continuous and nowhere zero, hence of constant sign ([F9]); since $\wp(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to0^+$ by the principal part in [F1] and $\wp(c_1)=e_1$, this sign is negative and $\wp$ decreases strictly from $+\infty$ to $e_1$. Likewise along the open segment from $c_1$ to $c_3$ and from $c_3$ to $c_2$ and from $c_2$ to $0$, all lying on the real locus lines, $\wp$ takes real values with nowhere-zero derivative and is thus strictly monotone; the segment from $c_2$ to $0$ is the imaginary interval because $c_2=ib/2$, and $\wp(iy)\to-\infty$ as $y\to0^+$ by [F1], so there $\wp$ decreases to $-\infty$. Because $\wp'(c_j)=0$ ([F2]), Taylor expansion at $c_j$ using [F3] gives $\wp(c_j+w)=e_j+\tfrac12\wp''(c_j)w^2+O(|w|^3)$ with $\wp''(c_j)=6e_j^2-g_2/2$ and, comparing the expansions of both sides of $(\wp')^2=4(\wp-e_1)(\wp-e_2)(\wp-e_3)$, $\wp''(c_j)=2\prod_{i\ne j}(e_j-e_i)$. At $c_1$ the incident edge towards $0$ has values $>e_1$ and the incident edge towards $c_3$ has values $<e_1$ (both signs by the second-order expansion, whose quadratic coefficient for the first edge is $+\wp''(c_1)/2$ and for the second $-\wp''(c_1)/2$), so $e_3<e_1$. At $c_2$ the incident edge towards $0$ has values $<e_2$ and the incident edge towards $c_3$ has values $>e_2$, so $e_3>e_2$. Hence $e_2<e_3<e_1$. [F1, F2, F3, F9, step 1.1]

2.3 (Boundary values of $q$ and $I_k$.) With the principal square roots of the four factors, the normalized root on $H$ is $q(z)=\sqrt{1-z}\sqrt{1+z}\sqrt{1-kz}\sqrt{1+kz}$: each factor is holomorphic on $H$, their product squares to $P$ and has positive boundary value on $(-1,1)$, so it is the root fixed in step 1.3. This formula also supplies its boundary continuation away from the four zeros. A negative value of $1-x$ or $1-kx$ is approached from below and contributes $-i$ times its positive absolute square root; a negative value of $1+x$ or $1+kx$ is approached from above and contributes $+i$ times that root. Thus $q(x+i0)=\sqrt{P(x)}$ for $-1<x<1$, $q(x+i0)=-i\sqrt{|P(x)|}$ for $1<x<1/k$, $q(x+i0)=+i\sqrt{|P(x)|}$ for $-1/k<x<-1$, and $q(x+i0)=-\sqrt{P(x)}$ on both tails $|x|>1/k$. Hence, using $I_k'(x+i0)=1/q(x+i0)$ and $I_k(0)=0$: $I_k$ is strictly increasing on $(-1,1)$ with $I_k(\pm1)=\pm K$; $I_k(x)=K+i\int_1^x ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(1-k^2s^2)}$ for $1\le x\le 1/k$, so $I_k(1/k)=K+iK'(k)$ where $K'(k)=\int_1^{1/k}ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(1-k^2s^2)}$; $I_k(x)=-K+i\int_x^{-1}ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(1-k^2s^2)}$ for $-1/k\le x\le-1$, so $I_k(-1/k)=-K+iK'(k)$; and on the tails $I_k(x)=I_k(1/k)-\int_{1/k}^x ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(k^2s^2-1)}$ and $I_k(x)=I_k(-1/k)+\int_x^{-1/k}ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(k^2s^2-1)}$, with $\int_{1/k}^{\infty}ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(k^2s^2-1)}=K$ and $\int_{-\infty}^{-1/k}ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(k^2s^2-1)}=K$, so both tails tend to $iK'(k)$. Here $\int_1^{1/k}ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(1-k^2s^2)}=K(\sqrt{1-k^2})=K'$ under the substitution $s=(1-k'^2u^2)^{-1/2}$ with $k'=\sqrt{1-k^2}$, and $\int_{1/k}^{\infty}ds/\sqrt{(s^2-1)(k^2s^2-1)}=K$ under $s=1/(ku)$, both by the change-of-variables formula ([F9]). Finally, for $|z|=R>1/k$ in $H$ one has $|P(z)|\ge(R^2-1)(k^2R^2-1)$, so the integral of $1/q$ along the semicircle of radius $R$ is $O(1/R)$; since $I_k(R)\to iK'(k)$ along the real axis, $I_k(z)\to iK'(k)$ uniformly as $|z|\to\infty$ in $H$. [F4, F8, F9, step 1.3]

3.1 (The image lies in one half-plane.) $S^\circ$ is convex, hence connected, and $\wp(S^\circ)$ is connected; since $\wp'\ne0$ on $S^\circ$, $\wp$ is an open map there and $\wp(S^\circ)$ is open ([F10]); and $\wp(S^\circ)\cap\mathbb R=\varnothing$ by step 2.1, because no interior point lies on any of the lines $\operatorname{Re}z\in\tfrac\alpha2\mathbb Z$, $\operatorname{Im}z\in\tfrac b2\mathbb Z$. An open connected subset of $\mathbb C\setminus(\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\})$ is contained in the upper or in the lower half-plane. [F4, step 2.1, step 1.2]

3.2 (The boundary maps onto $\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$.) By step 2.2 the four open edges have images $(e_1,\infty)$, the interval between $e_1$ and $e_3$, the interval between $e_3$ and $e_2$, and $(-\infty,e_2)$, and with $e_2<e_3<e_1$ these intervals are $(e_1,\infty)$, $(e_3,e_1)$, $(e_2,e_3)$ and $(-\infty,e_2)$, which together with the endpoint values and $\wp(0)=\infty$ cover $\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$ exactly once on the boundary circle. [F1, step 2.2]

3.3 (A closed-contour count for the Jacobi rectangle.) Write $R_0=(-K,K)\times(0,K')$ and $v=iK'$. At a real zero $a$ of $P$, local factorisation gives $1/q(z)=(z-a)^{-1/2}h(z)$ with $h$ holomorphic and nonzero; integration gives $I_k(z)=I_k(a)+O(|z-a|^{1/2})$. Thus $I_k$ extends continuously to the real axis, including the four branch points, and its boundary images are rectifiable. For large $R$, let $L_R$ be the full closed image of the positively oriented boundary of the upper half-disc of radius $R$. Its real-axis part goes from $A_R=I_k(-R)$ along the top-left, left, bottom and right edges to $B_R=I_k(R)$ on the top-right; its semicircle part returns from $B_R$ to $A_R$. By step 2.3, both this return path and the missing top segment from $B_R$ to $A_R$ lie in a disc about $v$ of radius tending to zero. Fix $w\notin\partial R_0$ and take $R$ large enough that this disc misses $w$. Replacing the return path by the top segment through a straight homotopy within that disc makes $L_R$ the counterclockwise rectangle boundary, so [F6] gives its winding number about $w$ as one if $w\in R_0$ and zero if $w\notin\overline{R_0}$.

To apply the argument principle entirely inside $H$, use $D_{R,\epsilon}=\{z:|z|<R,\ \operatorname{Im}z>\epsilon\}$ with $\epsilon>0$. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, parametrise its closed boundary compatibly with the half-disc boundary. Continuity of $I_k$ on the compact closed half-disc gives uniform convergence of the image loops to $L_R$. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$ the straight homotopy between these loops avoids $w$, so their winding numbers agree. The function $I_k$ is holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\overline{D_{R,\epsilon}}$, and [F6] counts its preimages of $w$ there: one for $w\in R_0$, zero for $w\notin\overline{R_0}$. All zeros are simple since $I_k'\ne0$. Exhausting $H$ by arbitrarily large $R$ and arbitrarily small $\epsilon$ proves exactly one preimage for every interior $w$ and none for every exterior $w$. No boundary value can be attained inside $H$: $I_k'\ne0$ makes its image open, so such a preimage would also produce an exterior value. Therefore $I_k(H)=R_0$, and $I_k$ is biholomorphic by [F10]. [F6, F8, F10, step 1.3, step 2.3]

4.1 (The image of $S$ is exactly one half-plane and $\wp|_S$ is conformal.) Every boundary point of $\wp(S^\circ)$ is a limit $\wp(z_n)$ with $z_n\in S^\circ$; by compactness of $\overline S$ pass to a subsequence with $z_n\to z_0\in\overline S$ and $\wp(z_0)=w$ with the value $\wp(0)=\infty$ allowed. If $z_0\in S^\circ$ then $w\in\wp(S^\circ)$, which is impossible for a boundary point because $\wp(S^\circ)$ is open; hence $z_0\in\partial S$ and, by step 3.2, $w\in\wp(\partial S)\subseteq\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$. Thus $\partial\wp(S^\circ)\subseteq\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$, while by step 3.1 the set $\wp(S^\circ)$ is a nonempty open connected subset of one half-plane $U_\pm$, and $U_\pm\cap(\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\})=\varnothing$. If $w\in U_\pm\setminus\wp(S^\circ)$, join $w$ to a point $q\in\wp(S^\circ)$ by the segment $\gamma$ inside the convex set $U_\pm$ and let $t_0=\inf\{t:\gamma(t)\in\wp(S^\circ)\}$; then $\gamma(t_0)\in\partial\wp(S^\circ)\cap U_\pm$, contradicting $\partial\wp(S^\circ)\subseteq\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$. Hence $\wp(S^\circ)=U_\pm$, and $\wp:S^\circ\to U_\pm$ is injective with nowhere-zero derivative, hence biholomorphic, and in particular conformal. [F10, step 3.1, step 3.2]

5.1 (Derivative of the inverse branch.) Let $U=U_\pm$ and $f=\wp|_{S^\circ}^{-1}:U\to S^\circ$. Then $f$ is holomorphic, $\wp(f(\zeta))=\zeta$ for $\zeta\in U$, and the chain rule gives $\wp'(f(\zeta))f'(\zeta)=1$, so $f'(\zeta)=1/\wp'(f(\zeta))$. Substituting $\wp(f(\zeta))=\zeta$ in the differential equation [F3] gives $\wp'(f(\zeta))^2=4\zeta^3-g_2\zeta-g_3$, and since $f'$ is nowhere zero its reciprocal $\zeta\mapsto 1/f'(\zeta)=\wp'(f(\zeta))$ is a holomorphic square root of $4\zeta^3-g_2\zeta-g_3$ on $U$; writing $(4\zeta^3-g_2\zeta-g_3)^{-1/2}$ for that reciprocal root, every inverse branch satisfies $f'(\zeta)=(4\zeta^3-g_2\zeta-g_3)^{-1/2}$. [F3, step 4.1]

6.1 (The four period integrals.) On each of the four real intervals between consecutive roots the polynomial $4x^3-g_2x-g_3=4(x-e_1)(x-e_2)(x-e_3)$ has constant sign; $4x^3-g_2x-g_3>0$ on $(e_1,\infty)$ and on $(e_2,e_3)$, while $g_3+g_2x-4x^3>0$ on $(-\infty,e_2)$ and on $(e_3,e_1)$. Each of these intervals is the image under $\wp$ of one open edge of $\partial S$, and the inverse branch $f$ maps it bijectively onto that edge with $|f'(x)|=1/\sqrt{|4x^3-g_2x-g_3|}$ by step 5.1, so the integral of the positive square root over the interval equals the length of the corresponding displacement: writing the inverse branch as $g$, $\int_a^b dx/\sqrt{|4x^3-g_2x-g_3|}=|\lim_{x\downarrow a}g(x)-\lim_{x\uparrow b}g(x)|$ by the change-of-variables formula and strict monotonicity of $g$ ([F9]). The four displacements are: from $0$ to $c_1$, length $\alpha/2$; from $c_2$ to $c_3$, length $\alpha/2$; from $c_2$ to $0$, length $|\beta|/2=\beta/(2i)$; from $c_1$ to $c_3$, length $\beta/(2i)$. Hence the four displayed identities hold with the positive real square roots. [F1, F2, F3, F9, step 2.2, step 3.2, step 5.1]

7.1 (The inverse sn and its double periodicity.) Let $\mathrm{sn}=I_k^{-1}:R_0\to H$; it is holomorphic ([F10]) and continuous on $\overline{R_0}\setminus\{iK'\}$ with real boundary values: the bottom edge $[-K,K]$ maps into $(-1,1)$ with $\mathrm{sn}(0)=0$, $\mathrm{sn}(\pm K)=\pm1$; the left edge $-K+i(0,K')$ maps into $(-1/k,-1)$ with $\mathrm{sn}(-K+iK')=-1/k$; the right edge $K+i(0,K')$ maps into $(1,1/k)$ with $\mathrm{sn}(K+iK')=1/k$; and the top edge $(-K,K)+iK'$ maps into $\mathbb R$ with $|\mathrm{sn}|>1/k$, with a simple pole at $iK'$ (from step 2.3, $I_k(z)=iK'+1/(kz)+O(z^{-2})$ for large $z$, so near the omitted value $iK'$ the inverse behaves like $1/(k(w-iK'))$). At each corner $w_a=I_k(a)$ with $a=\pm1,\pm1/k$, the local form $I_k(z)=w_a+(z-a)^{1/2}h_a(z)$ with $h_a(a)\ne0$ gives an inverse $z=a+O((w-w_a)^2)$ holomorphic across the corner; this also makes adjacent reflections agree there. Since $\mathrm{sn}$ is holomorphic on $R_0$ and real on each of the four open sides, the Schwarz reflection principle [F7] extends it across each side by reflection there: away from $iK'$ this is the stated holomorphic reflection, and at $iK'$ one applies the same principle to the reciprocal $u=1/\mathrm{sn}$, which is holomorphic near $iK'$ with $u(iK')=0$ and real boundary values, so $u$ reflects and $\mathrm{sn}=1/u$ reflects meromorphically; the reflected copies tile the plane, because the four reflections $\sigma_b(z)=\overline z$, $\sigma_t(z)=\overline z+2iK'$, $\sigma_l(z)=-2K-\overline z$, $\sigma_r(z)=2K-\overline z$ generate the group generated by the translations $\sigma_b\sigma_t:z\mapsto z-2iK'$ and $\sigma_r\sigma_l:z\mapsto z+4K$, whose orbits of the rectangle tile the plane. The resulting single meromorphic function $\mathrm{sn}$ on $\mathbb C$ satisfies $\mathrm{sn}(\sigma_jz)=\overline{\mathrm{sn}(z)}$ for each reflection $\sigma_j$, so $\mathrm{sn}(z-2iK')=\overline{\mathrm{sn}(\sigma_tz)}=\mathrm{sn}(z)$ and $\mathrm{sn}(z+4K)=\overline{\mathrm{sn}(\sigma_lz)}=\mathrm{sn}(z)$: $\mathrm{sn}$ is doubly periodic with periods $4K$ and $2iK'$ (and period $2iK'$ implies period $-2iK'$). ∎

## Remarks

The sign analysis is the only delicate point. The normalized square root $q$ of $(1-\zeta^2)(1-k^2\zeta^2)$ is positive on $(-1,1)$, and the local factorizations at $\pm1$ and $\pm1/k$ force the boundary values $-i\sqrt{|P|}$ on $(1,1/k)$, $+i\sqrt{|P|}$ on $(-1/k,-1)$, and $-\sqrt{P}$ on both tails; the two tails then approach the same point $iK'$, which is what closes the image of the real axis into the boundary of the rectangle. The same computation for $\wp$ gives $e_2<e_3<e_1$ directly from the second-order expansions at $c_1$ and $c_2$; no numerical evaluation of any elliptic integral is used, only the two standard substitutions reducing $K'(k)$ to $K(\sqrt{1-k^2})$ and the tail integral to $K$ itself.
